Unreasonable
un-rē'zn-a-bl
adj. (contrary to reason, or without reason; used by Festus of a procedural absurdity and by Paul of men from whom he asks to be delivered)
From un- and reasonable, Latin ratio. In Acts 25:27 the Greek is alogos, without reason, illogical; in 2 Thessalonians 3:2 the word is atopos, literally out of place, hence improper or absurd.

Biblical Definition

Festus, having to send Paul to Rome and unable to formulate a charge, says: “For it seemeth to me unreasonable to send a prisoner, and not withal to signify the crimes laid against him” (Acts 25:27). It is an admission of the whole case's emptiness — the governor cannot state what the man is accused of, and knows how that will look at the imperial court. Paul uses a different word for a different thing when he asks the Thessalonians to pray “that we may be delivered from unreasonable and wicked men: for all men have not faith” (2 Thessalonians 3:2). The Greek there means out of place, absurd, perverse — men with whom argument does not work, because the obstacle is not intellectual. The clause that follows explains it: for all men have not faith. Opposition to the gospel is not finally a failure of information. And Paul does not end on the danger: “But the Lord is faithful, who shall stablish you, and keep you from evil” (2 Thessalonians 3:3). Men are unreasonable; the Lord is faithful; the sentence turns on that contrast.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines unreasonable as not agreeable to reason, exceeding the bounds of reason, immoderate, and also not conformable to reason in conduct.

expand to see more

UNREASONABLE, a. Not agreeable to reason.

2. Exceeding the bounds of reason; claiming or insisting on more than is fit; as an unreasonable demand.

3. Immoderate; as unreasonable bulk.

4. Irrational; as unreasonable creatures.

ABSURD, a. Opposed to manifest truth; inconsistent with reason or the plain dictates of common sense.

Key Scripture

Acts 25:27 — "For it seemeth to me unreasonable to send a prisoner, and not withal to signify the crimes laid against him."

2 Thessalonians 3:2 — "And that we may be delivered from unreasonable and wicked men: for all men have not faith."

2 Thessalonians 3:3 — "But the Lord is faithful, who shall stablish you, and keep you from evil."

Acts 25:16 — "To whom I answered, It is not the manner of the Romans to deliver any man to die, before that he which is accused have the accusers face to face, and have licence to answer for himself concerning the crime laid against him."

Modern Corruption

Unbelief is treated as an argument to be won, and Paul locates the obstacle where Scripture always locates it — in the will, not the intellect.

expand to see more

2 Thessalonians 3:2 is a short course in apologetics. Paul asks for deliverance from unreasonable and wicked men and then gives the diagnosis in five words: for all men have not faith. The men are not merely mistaken; they are without faith, and no quantity of argument supplies what only God gives. This does not make reasoning useless — Paul reasoned in the synagogues every sabbath, and Peter commands a reason for the hope that is in us. It means that argument is a means and not the cause, and that a Christian who has answered every objection and met a hardened response has encountered exactly what the apostle describes rather than a failure of technique.

Acts 25:27 shows the other side, where the unreasonableness is procedural and a pagan official is the one who notices it. Festus cannot name the crime and finds it absurd to forward a prisoner without one. Persecution frequently has this quality: enormous energy directed at a man whose offence, when someone finally tries to write it down, evaporates. Luke lets the point make itself — three separate officials in these chapters say Paul has done nothing worthy of death or bonds, and he is sent to Rome anyway. The record is not merely biographical; it is the earliest legal defence of Christianity, written down by a careful historian.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek alogos (G249), without reason, absurd — Acts 25:27, 2 Peter 2:12, Jude 10; atopos (G824), out of place, perverse — 2 Thessalonians 3:2, Luke 23:41, Acts 28:6.

expand to see more

Greek alogos (G249) — without reason, irrational; Acts 25:27, and 2 Peter 2:12 of natural brute beasts.

Greek atopos (G824) — out of place, improper, absurd; 2 Thessalonians 3:2, and Luke 23:41 where the thief says Christ hath done nothing amiss.

Greek pistis (G4102) — faith; 2 Thessalonians 3:2, all men have not faith.

Greek pistos (G4103) — faithful; 2 Thessalonians 3:3, the deliberate answering word in the next verse.

1 Corinthians 2:14 supplies the doctrine: the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God, neither can he know them.

Usage

"“Unreasonable to send a prisoner, and not withal to signify the crimes” — a governor with no charge."

"“Delivered from unreasonable and wicked men: for all men have not faith”."

"“But the Lord is faithful” — the contrast the sentence turns on."
